aeo.what_is: A mood condition with periods of elevated energy and mood alternating with episodes of deep depression, without full-blown mania.

content.temporal_criteria: A hypomanic episode lasts at least four consecutive days with elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased energy. Major depressive episodes last at least two weeks. The diagnosis requires at least one lifetime hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, with no history of full mania. People often spend more time depressed than hypomanic.

confused_with: Major Depressive Disorder — when depression dominates and hypomania is subtle or not asked about, people may be diagnosed with unipolar depression and treated with antidepressants alone, which can worsen cycling.
Bipolar I Disorder — hypomania is sometimes mistaken for mania, but hypomania is shorter (4+ days vs. 7+ days), less severe, doesn't require hospitalization, and doesn't include psychosis.

ADHD — chronic restlessness and distractibility from childhood differ from distinct hypomanic episodes with elevated mood, decreased sleep need, and increased goal-directed activity emerging later in life.
Borderline Personality Disorder — BPD mood swings are rapid (hours) and triggered by interpersonal events, while bipolar hypomania lasts days and often occurs without clear triggers.

Cyclothymic Disorder — cyclothymia involves chronic subthreshold mood swings without full hypomanic or depressive episodes; Bipolar II requires meeting full criteria for both hypomania and major depression.
misdiagnosis_explained.clarifying_factors: Detailed history of distinct mood episodes with clear start and end points; collateral from family/friends who noticed 'up' periods; asking about times of decreased sleep with high energy (not just insomnia); screening for spending sprees, increased socializing, or bursts of productivity; distinguishing chronic traits from episodic changes.
misdiagnosis_explained.timeline_differences: ADHD and personality patterns are stable across the lifespan. Bipolar II involves episodic changes: periods of normal functioning punctuated by hypomania or depression. MDD has depressive episodes without hypomanic periods. Cyclothymia has fluctuations that never reach full episode thresholds.
misdiagnosis_explained.impairment_differences: Major depression causes severe functional impairment and withdrawal. Hypomania often feels good and may enhance productivity initially, but it precedes or follows disabling depression. BPD mood shifts cause distress but typically don't include the decreased sleep need and sustained elevated energy seen in hypomania.

description.overview: Bipolar II Disorder is characterized by at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, with no history of a full manic episode. Hypomania features elevated/expansive or irritable mood and increased energy lasting at least 4 consecutive days, observable by others, with clear change from baseline but without marked impairment, hospitalization, or psychosis.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A 24-year-old grad student who's been depressed for months suddenly has a four-day stretch where she sleeps only four hours, feels energized, reorganizes her entire apartment at 2 a.m., and signs up for three new projects. Her friends notice she's 'back to herself,' but then she crashes into another depressive episode.

A 30-year-old accountant experiences recurrent depressions but never mentions the occasional weeks when he needs less sleep, works late into the night on side projects, feels unusually confident, and sends enthusiastic late-night texts to friends. His doctor treats him for depression alone until a careful history reveals the pattern.

A 28-year-old teacher has five-day periods where she's chattier than usual, stays up late planning elaborate lessons, buys classroom supplies she doesn't need, and feels 'on top of the world.' Then she sinks into weeks of fatigue, hopelessness, and calling in sick.

A 35-year-old designer cycles between intense creative bursts where he barely sleeps, pitches bold ideas to clients, and feels unstoppable, and long stretches where he can't get out of bed, doubts his abilities, and isolates from friends.

A 26-year-old has been diagnosed with depression for years. After a detailed timeline, her therapist realizes that between depressive episodes, she has brief periods of high energy, increased socializing, impulsive online shopping, and feeling like she 'doesn't need much sleep'—all signs of hypomania she'd dismissed as 'finally feeling normal.'

A 40-year-old notices he gets 'wound up' for a few days every few months—talking fast, starting multiple hobbies, feeling irritable when others can't keep up—but it never lasts long and he always thought it was just stress. The depressive crashes afterward are what brought him to treatment.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief that the pattern of 'good weeks' and 'bad months' finally has a name.
Confusion about why hypomania is considered part of an illness when it feels so much better than depression.
Frustration that past treatment with antidepressants alone didn't address the cycling.
Grief about needing long-term treatment and lifestyle changes.
Fear that mood stabilizers will flatten the energized, productive periods.
Validation that they weren't 'just lazy' during depressions or 'overreacting' during hypomanic irritability.
Concern about disclosing the diagnosis to employers, partners, or family.

content.diagnostic_criteria: A. ≥1 hypomanic episode and ≥1 major depressive episode. B. No history of manic episode. C. Hypomanic episode: ≥4 days of elevated/expansive/irritable mood and increased energy plus ≥3 (≥4 if mood only irritable) of: inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity/psychomotor agitation, risky activities. D. Major depressive episode criteria met. E. Symptoms are not better explained by another mental disorder, substance, or medical condition and cause clinically significant distress or impairment.
content.prevalence: Lifetime ~1–2%; often underrecognized due to subtle or ego-syntonic hypomania and prominent depression.
content.age_of_onset: Late adolescence to early adulthood; depressive episodes frequently precede recognition of hypomania.
content.prognosis: Recurrent episodes with greater time spent in depression than hypomania. Early identification, maintenance mood stabilization, psychotherapy, and circadian regularity reduce relapse, suicidality, and functional impairment.

circuitry: Fronto-limbic dysregulation (ventromedial/dorsolateral prefrontal cortex–amygdala–anterior cingulate) affecting emotion regulation and reward.
Striatal and thalamo-cortical network alterations linked to goal-directed activity and sleep–wake rhythms.
neurochemistry: Monoaminergic perturbations (dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine) with state-dependent changes.
Glutamate/GABA imbalance and inflammatory/HPA-axis signaling differences.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: High polygenic heritability; circadian disruption, stress, and substances (stimulants, cannabis, alcohol) act as triggers.

history_psychosocial: Longitudinal timeline emphasizing hypomanic symptoms (reduced sleep without fatigue, increased productivity/sociability, spending) and major depressions.
Family history of bipolar spectrum; trauma/stressors; substance use patterns.
medical_assessment: Rule out secondary causes/substances (steroids, stimulants, thyroid disease).
Screen labs: CBC, CMP, TSH; pregnancy test when relevant; ECG if cardiac risk with antipsychotics.
standardized_measures: Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) adapted for hypomania; Hypomania Checklist (HCL-32); PHQ-9 or MADRS for depression.
Mood Disorder Questionnaire (MDQ) for lifetime features; C-SSRS for suicide risk.
risk_stratification: Hospitalize for severe depression with suicidality, psychosis, catatonia, or inability to care for self; or if hypomania escalates toward mania/unsafe behavior.
differential_diagnosis: Borderline Personality Disorder (affect reactivity to interpersonal stress vs. episodic mood elevation).
Substance/medication-induced mood disorder; medical causes (hyperthyroidism, Cushing’s).
evaluation.team_and_process: Collaborative care with psychiatry and primary care; include family/partners for collateral and relapse planning; coordinate OB-GYN or neurology as needed.

hypomania: Decreased need for sleep with increased energy/productivity
Heightened sociability, goal-directed activity, or irritability
Risk-taking (spending, driving, sex) without marked impairment
associated_features: Rapid cycling in a subset; anxiety disorders common; mixed features possible

severity_levels.mild: Symptoms noticeable but manageable; limited functional impact; outpatient care.
severity_levels.moderate: Clear impairment across roles; intensive outpatient or partial hospital may be indicated.
severity_levels.severe: Severe depression, suicidality, or near-manic escalation; inpatient care often required.

environmental: Shift work, jet lag, chronic stress

impact_on_life.school_work: Absenteeism and reduced productivity during depression; risky decisions or overcommitment during hypomania.
impact_on_life.social: Interpersonal conflict from irritability or impulsivity; guilt/shame during depressive phases.
impact_on_life.medical: Weight/metabolic effects of medications; sleep disruption; accidents with risk behaviors.
impact_on_life.emotional: Demoralization and anxiety about future episodes; elevated suicide risk (notably during depression/mixed states).

comorbidities: Anxiety disorders (GAD, panic, PTSD, social anxiety)

acute_bipolar_depression: Lamotrigine (modest acute benefit; stronger for prevention).
Olanzapine–fluoxetine combination in adults when appropriate.
Avoid antidepressant monotherapy; if used, combine with a mood stabilizer and monitor for switch.
hypomania_management: Optimize sleep and reduce stimulation; brief benzodiazepine adjunct for insomnia/agitation.
Lithium or valproate; atypical antipsychotics (e.g., quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole) when needed.
maintenance_relapse_prevention: Lithium (suicide risk reduction); lamotrigine; quetiapine; valproate in selected cases.
Monitor for rapid cycling and mixed features; address thyroid/substance contributors.
psychotherapy: Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy (IPSRT) for circadian stabilization.
CBT for bipolar depression and adherence; relapse prevention planning.
Family-Focused Therapy (FFT) to reduce expressed emotion; DBT skills for emotion regulation/impulsivity.
neuromodulation: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) for severe, psychotic, or treatment-resistant depression or suicidality.
Repetitive TMS as adjunct for bipolar depression (specialist-guided).
lifestyle_interventions: Strict sleep–wake routines; light hygiene; avoid night shifts.
Limit alcohol/cannabis/stimulants; regular aerobic activity and nutrition.
Digital mood/sleep tracking; stimulus control during hypomanic drift.
medications: Mood stabilizers: lithium, lamotrigine, valproate/divalproex (selected cases), carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine (second-line).
Atypical antipsychotics: quetiapine, lurasidone, cariprazine, olanzapine (often with fluoxetine), risperidone/aripiprazole for hypomania control.
Monitoring: lithium levels/renal/thyroid; valproate levels/LFTs/platelets; antipsychotic metabolic labs; lamotrigine rash monitoring (slow titration).
Reproductive considerations: avoid valproate in pregnancy when possible; discuss contraception and perinatal plans.
care_coordination: Safety planning and suicide risk management.
Shared decision-making; advance directives for relapse signatures.
With consent, involve family/supports and coordinate school/work accommodations.

treatment_goals: Resolve bipolar depression and control hypomanic symptoms.
Prevent relapse/rapid cycling and reduce suicide risk.
Minimize adverse effects and protect physical health.
Restore functioning and quality of life with sustainable routines.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Presenting only with recurrent depression; hypomania not elicited or seen as ‘good days’.
Attributing reduced sleep/energy changes to work or ADHD without assessing euphoria/irritability and episodicity.
Substance use obscuring hypomania; brief hypomania after antidepressants not explored.
overdiagnosis_factors: Labeling MDD with agitation or brief stress reactivity as hypomania.
Diagnosing on the basis of stimulant/caffeine intoxication or sleep deprivation without sustained syndrome.
Using positive MDQ alone without clinical interview; confusing BPD affective lability with episodic hypomania.

features: With mood-congruent or mood-incongruent psychotic features (psychosis implies mania → re-evaluate for Bipolar I)

warning_signs: Decreasing sleep need with rising energy and goal-directed activity.
Escalating spending/risk-taking, irritability, or pressured socializing.
Worsening hopelessness, anhedonia, or suicidality during depressive phases.
self_help_strategies: Keep consistent sleep–wake times; avoid night shifts and jet lag.
Track early signs (sleep, spending, sociability); share a plan with supports.
Use reminders/pill organizers; attend scheduled follow-ups.

adolescence: Often presents as recurrent depression with subtle hypomania; family involvement and school accommodations help adherence and sleep regularity.
young_adulthood: Transitions (college/work/relationships) challenge routines; IPSRT and CBT support rhythm stability and adherence.
midlife_older_adults: Comorbid medical illness and polypharmacy considerations; monitor renal/thyroid (lithium), metabolic risk with SGAs, and drug interactions.

first_person_statements: I thought the hypomania was just me finally feeling good, but my therapist helped me see it was part of the cycle that led to crushing depressions.
People loved me when I was hypomanic—I was fun, energetic, the life of the party—but I paid for it with weeks of not being able to function.
I didn't realize how little I was sleeping during those 'productive' weeks until I started tracking my mood and sleep. That's when the pattern became clear.
The hardest part was accepting that even the 'good' periods were part of the illness and needed treatment, not just the depressions.
Bipolar II felt like being on a roller coaster I couldn't get off: the highs were exhilarating but short, and the lows were devastating and long.
I spent years being treated for depression, and antidepressants alone made me cycle faster. Getting the right diagnosis changed everything.

comparisons: It's like a seesaw that tips gently upward for a few days (hypomania) and then crashes down hard for weeks or months (depression), never quite staying level.

Imagine your brain's energy switch gets stuck on 'high' for a few days—you're wired, productive, and don't need much sleep—and then flips to 'low' for weeks, leaving you exhausted and unable to enjoy anything.
Think of it as a softer version of Bipolar I's roller coaster: the ups are noticeable but not extreme, while the downs are just as deep and disabling as any major depression.
It's like living with two different operating systems: one runs fast, feels confident, and needs little rest, and the other barely boots up, doubts everything, and can't sustain even basic tasks.

faqs.question: What's the difference between Bipolar I and Bipolar II?
faqs.answer: Bipolar I involves at least one full manic episode (severe, often requiring hospitalization, possibly with psychosis). Bipolar II involves hypomania (milder, shorter, no hospitalization or psychosis) plus major depression. Both are serious, but Bipolar I has more severe highs.

faqs.question: How is Bipolar II different from Major Depressive Disorder?
faqs.answer: MDD involves depressive episodes without any hypomanic or manic periods. Bipolar II includes both depression and hypomania. The distinction matters because treatment differs: antidepressants alone can worsen Bipolar II, while mood stabilizers are key.

faqs.question: Is hypomania dangerous?
faqs.answer: Hypomania is less dangerous than mania—it doesn't include psychosis or require hospitalization—but it can still lead to impulsive decisions (overspending, risky behavior, relationship conflicts) and often precedes or follows severe depression. It's part of a larger pattern that needs treatment.

faqs.question: Can Bipolar II turn into Bipolar I?
faqs.answer: It's possible but not common. If someone with Bipolar II ever has a full manic episode, the diagnosis changes to Bipolar I. Most people with Bipolar II remain in that category, though stressors, substances, or medication changes can sometimes trigger more severe episodes.

faqs.question: Why do I spend more time depressed than hypomanic?
faqs.answer: That's typical for Bipolar II. Hypomanic episodes are usually brief (days to a week or two), while depressive episodes last weeks to months. Most people with Bipolar II experience depression as the dominant and most impairing phase.

faqs.question: Do I need medication if I only feel bad during depression?
faqs.answer: Yes, because the hypomania and depression are part of the same cycling disorder. Mood stabilizers or certain medications help prevent both the depressive and hypomanic episodes, reducing the frequency and severity of the cycle overall.

faqs.question: Can therapy alone treat Bipolar II?
faqs.answer: Therapy is very helpful for managing stress, recognizing early warning signs, and maintaining routines, but it's usually not sufficient alone. Most people with Bipolar II need medication (mood stabilizers or certain atypicals) to prevent cycling, plus therapy for the best outcomes.

faqs.question: Will mood stabilizers make me feel flat or numb?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. The goal is to reduce extreme swings while preserving your ability to feel happiness, sadness, and motivation. Some people experience side effects initially, but adjustments can often find a balance that feels stable without being flat.

faqs.question: Can antidepressants make Bipolar II worse?
faqs.answer: Yes. Antidepressants without a mood stabilizer can trigger hypomania, increase cycling, or lead to mixed states. If antidepressants are used, they're typically combined with a mood stabilizer and monitored carefully.

faqs.question: What triggers hypomanic episodes?
faqs.answer: Common triggers include sleep disruption, stopping medication, high stress, antidepressant use without a mood stabilizer, seasonal changes, and substance use (especially stimulants). Some episodes occur without obvious triggers.

faqs.question: How do I know if I'm hypomanic or just in a good mood?
faqs.answer: Hypomania includes decreased need for sleep (feeling fine on much less), increased energy and activity, talkativeness, racing thoughts, and often impulsive decisions—sustained over days. A good mood doesn't disrupt sleep or lead to risky behavior.

faqs.question: Is Bipolar II genetic?
faqs.answer: Yes, there's a strong genetic component. Having a first-degree relative with bipolar disorder or major depression increases risk. However, it's not a single gene—many genetic variants plus environmental factors (stress, substance use) interact.

faqs.question: Can I work or go to school with Bipolar II?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Many people with Bipolar II work and study successfully with proper treatment, consistent routines, and accommodations when needed (flexible deadlines during rough patches, for example). Stability is achievable with the right support.

faqs.question: What should I do if I think I'm becoming hypomanic?
faqs.answer: Contact your treatment team as soon as possible. Early signs include needing less sleep without feeling tired, increased activity, rapid speech, or impulsive decisions. Adjusting medication, prioritizing sleep, and reducing stimulation can sometimes prevent escalation.

faqs.question: Can substance use cause Bipolar II?
faqs.answer: Substance use doesn't cause Bipolar II, but stimulants, alcohol, and cannabis can trigger or worsen episodes in vulnerable individuals. Many people with Bipolar II struggle with substances, which complicates diagnosis and treatment.

faqs.question: What's rapid cycling in Bipolar II?
faqs.answer: Rapid cycling means having four or more mood episodes (hypomanic or depressive) within a year. It's harder to treat and often linked to factors like antidepressant use without mood stabilizers, thyroid issues, or substance use.

faqs.question: Can Bipolar II get better with age?
faqs.answer: Episode frequency can sometimes decrease with age, especially with consistent treatment. However, untreated Bipolar II often worsens, with more frequent episodes and longer recovery times. Early, sustained treatment improves long-term outcomes.

faqs.question: What's the suicide risk in Bipolar II?
faqs.answer: Bipolar II has a high suicide risk, particularly during depressive episodes. The combination of severe depression and a history of impulsive behavior during hypomania increases risk. Mood stabilizers like lithium have been shown to reduce suicide risk.

faqs.question: How long do I need to take medication?
faqs.answer: Most people with Bipolar II need long-term treatment to prevent relapse. Stopping medication is a common cause of recurrence. Some may attempt cautious tapers after years of stability, but this requires close monitoring and should be discussed with your treatment team.

faqs.question: Can sleep disruption trigger episodes?
faqs.answer: Yes. Sleep disruption is one of the most common triggers for both hypomanic and depressive episodes. Maintaining a consistent sleep schedule is one of the most important self-care strategies for Bipolar II.

real_life_examples.person: A 22-year-old college senior with a history of two severe depressions mentioned to her psychiatrist that after finals week she had a five-day stretch where she slept only three hours a night, felt great, deep-cleaned her apartment, signed up for a marathon, and texted friends constantly. Her doctor recognized this as hypomania. She started quetiapine for the current depression and lamotrigine for prevention. IPSRT helped her stabilize sleep and routines, and she completed her degree without further episodes.

A 35-year-old software developer experienced recurrent depressions every few months. Between episodes, he'd have week-long bursts of high energy where he'd code all night, feel 'in the zone,' and make impulsive online purchases. After a careful history, his psychiatrist diagnosed Bipolar II. Lithium and CBT for relapse prevention reduced cycling. Stopping nightly cannabis use and maintaining a strict sleep schedule made a dramatic difference.

A 28-year-old teacher was treated for depression with an SSRI for two years. She kept cycling into brief hypomanic periods with irritability, racing thoughts, and insomnia, followed by deeper depressions. Her psychiatrist recognized the pattern, stopped the SSRI, and started lamotrigine. With sleep tracking and therapy, she's been stable for 18 months and returned to full-time teaching.

A 40-year-old graphic designer sought help after years of 'ups and downs.' She described feeling great for a few days—staying up late working on creative projects, feeling confident and social—then crashing into weeks of fatigue, self-doubt, and isolation. Quetiapine and IPSRT helped her recognize and manage early warning signs. She now uses a mood app and maintains consistent routines, with only one mild depressive episode in two years.

A 26-year-old nurse with recurrent depressions revealed during intake that she occasionally had four- or five-day periods where she felt 'amazing,' needed only four hours of sleep, took on extra shifts, and booked spontaneous weekend trips. Her doctor diagnosed Bipolar II and started lithium. With regular therapy and family support, she learned to spot early signs of hypomania (reduced sleep, increased spending) and adjust her schedule to prevent full episodes.

content.when_to_seek_help: Urgent care for suicidal ideation, psychosis, or near-manic escalation with unsafe behaviors. Seek prompt evaluation for new hypomanic symptoms, significant sleep reduction without fatigue, or depressive episodes impairing functioning.

positive_factors: Early maintenance with lithium/lamotrigine or evidence-based SGAs
Substance abstinence and strong social support
challenging_factors: Rapid cycling, mixed features, or comorbid anxiety/substance use
Irregular sleep, shift work, or poor adherence
High expressed emotion or ongoing psychosocial stressors
